data.title: Slavic hillforts in Austria (A) – guards on the frontier with the Eastern March
data.excerpt: As Drahoslav Hulínek notes in the volume Bitka pri Bratislave, the fortified settlements of Lower Austria north of the Danube were probably typical early medieval guard hillforts in the unstable borderland between the Moravian part of Great Moravia and the Eastern March. Six of them are described here, from Sand near Raabs, burnt down after a Magyar raid, to Langenlois-Schiltern.
data.metaTitle: Slavic hillforts in Austria – guards on the frontier
data.metaDescription: Early medieval Slavic guard hillforts in Lower Austria north of the Danube, in the borderland between Great Moravia and the Eastern March.

keyFacts.label: Hillforts described in Lower Austria
keyFacts.value: 6 sites – Sand near Raabs, Maissau-Limberg, Oberleis-Oberleiserberg, Stein an der Donau, Senftenberg, Langenlois-Schiltern

keyFacts.label: Sand near Raabs – northern ditch and wall
keyFacts.value: a ditch 2.4 m wide and 2 m deep, behind it a drystone wall about 2.4 m high

keyFacts.label: Sand near Raabs – elongated log building
keyFacts.value: just under 18 m long, 7 m wide at the eastern and 4 m at the western end, with a hearth in the middle

keyFacts.label: Sand near Raabs – demise of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: destroyed in about the third quarter of the 10th century after a Magyar raid and the ensuing fire

keyFacts.label: Oberleis-Oberleiserberg – elevation
keyFacts.value: 454 m above sea level; originally a prehistoric fortified settlement reused by the Slavs as a guard post

keyFacts.label: Maissau-Limberg – the Heidenstatt site
keyFacts.value: around 288 m above sea level; originally a prehistoric hillfort with predominantly pottery finds

keyFacts.label: Stein an der Donau and Senftenberg
keyFacts.value: both lie in the district of Krems an der Donau in the eastern Waldviertel and served a guard function

keyFacts.label: Find on the castle hill near Raabs
keyFacts.value: an area of 14 × 11 m with quarry stones – interpreted as a building with a stone footing and a timber superstructure

children.text: As Drahoslav Hulínek notes in the volume Bitka pri Bratislave (The Battle of Bratislava), the fortified settlements in the territory of Lower Austria north of the Danube were probably typical early medieval guard hillforts, spread across the wider frontier zone between the Moravian part of Great Moravia and the Eastern March. This was a territory unstable in political and power terms, in which the dominant role of a local centre was played by the already mentioned hillfort of
Gars/Thunau
. It was a territory very close to Moravia, and for some time it was also part of the Great Moravian state.
Sand near Raabs on the Dyje

The hillfort lies about 1.5 km from Raabs Castle, in the cadastral area of the village of Oberpfaffendorf. It is a small promontory site in a bend of the river Dyje. This Slavic hillfort may have served as a local centre, or possibly in a guard role, but it was established at the beginning of the 10th century. In about the third quarter of the 10th century it was apparently raided by the Magyars and was destroyed in a fire.
The structure of the hillfort and its fortification

The northern terrace was protected by ditches and ramparts. The ditch was 2.4 m wide and 2 m deep. Behind the ditch stood a wall of drystone masonry. The original height of the wall was about 2.4 m. Small timber houses stood directly against the inner face of this wall. In front of the lower settlement terrace, behind a berm, there was also a relatively shallow ditch, only a metre deep and three metres wide. In the second phase, however, it was filled in and a road paved with small quarry stones was laid out in its place. Ramparts were also present on the southern terrace. The outer one of them consisted of a stone wall with timber reinforcement. The inner face of the rampart was formed of horizontally laid beams. In places the construction rested on a timber grillage. Behind this fortification stood buildings without any heating installation. The inner rampart was formed of a 1.5 m wide drystone wall 2.4 m high. Post-built and log structures were again set against the wall, though not entirely continuously. At the western end of the terrace there was a gateway. On the western slope of the hillfort – the so-called Castle Hill (Burghügel) – there was a palisade and behind it a drystone wall, which again had dwellings built against it, joined to it casemate-fashion over a length of 2 m.
Buildings

The houses in the northern part of the promontory were built directly against the inner face of the rampart. On the western side there was a trapezoidal log building with domed ovens, attested by the remains of a beam. Adjoining this building on the eastern side is an elongated structure just under 18 m long. It was built of vertical posts and log walls. The house widens out towards the east in a trapezoidal fashion, and at its widest point there was a row of central posts. At the eastern end the house is 7 m wide, at the western end 4 m, and in the middle of the building there was a hearth.

The buildings were destroyed by a fire in which the wall collapsed onto the timber structures. After the fire, remains of charred wooden beams survived, coming mostly from the southern walls of the timber houses. In the western part of the rampart there was a timber structure 2.3 m wide on the inner face of the stone wall. Its northern wooden threshold was charred. North of the above-mentioned structure, and to the east directly against the inner face of the rampart, an occupation layer was uncovered, bounded on the north by a drystone wall that had largely collapsed. On its outer side the wall was accompanied by a paved road about a metre wide. In the middle of the terrace, towards the north, the settlement area widens. Post holes appear here, so it is quite likely that post-built structures also stood in these places.

On an area of 14 × 11 m on the castle hill, quarry stones were found which partly rested on the occupation layer. A number of large stones bounded the northern side. Archaeologists interpret the find as a building with a stone footing and a timber superstructure.
Further Slavic hillforts in Austria
Maissau-Limberg

The site at Maissau was originally a prehistoric hillfort, probably reused in the Early Middle Ages as a guard hillfort, or merely as a refuge. The hillfort lies at Limberg (around 288 m above sea level), which is administered by Maissau. The fortified settlement is located at the site known as Heidenstatt near Limberg. This site contained above all pottery finds, and its fortification cannot be regarded as early medieval in origin. It was originally a prehistoric fortified position, reoccupied by the Slavs in the Early Middle Ages. Its more precise social and military significance cannot as yet be determined with any certainty. Future research, however, may reveal new facts about this hillfort.
Oberleis-Oberleiserberg

The Lower Austrian site at Oberleis-Oberleiserberg (454 m above sea level), near the town of Korneuburg, north of Ernstbrunn, where there had originally been a prehistoric fortified settlement, was likewise reused by the Slavs in the Early Middle Ages as an important strategic guard post. Although Great Moravian finds occur there, as far as the fortifications are concerned, no early medieval Slavic origin was established when they were investigated. Any rebuilding of the defences in the Early Middle Ages is therefore not clearly attested.
Stein an der Donau

The fortified hillfort of Stein an der Donau (Lower Austria, district of Krems an der Donau) was probably built in the Early Middle Ages. It lies in the eastern Waldviertel, west of the town of Krems (around 199 m above sea level), and served a guard function. Territorially it belonged either to the Great Moravian state or to the transitional zone between Great Moravia and the Frankish political sphere.
Senftenberg

Another probable guard hillfort lay at Senftenberg (Lower Austria, district of Krems an der Donau). In all likelihood it was a fortified settlement built in the Early Middle Ages. It lay in a territory that may well have been part of Great Moravia in the 9th century, or was a transitional zone between the Eastern March, Bavaria and Moravia.
Langenlois-Schiltern

A hillfort was probably also built in the Early Middle Ages at Langenlois-Schiltern (around 219 m above sea level; district of Krems an der Donau), which lay in the eastern Waldviertel, north of Krems.
